passage_title: Clearing Time of a Cloudy Suspension Treated with Four Additives
passage:
A powdered solid stirred into water scatters light, so the water looks cloudy. As the particles settle or clump together, the cloudiness falls. Researchers defined the clearing time of a sample as the number of minutes for its cloudiness to fall to half the value measured just after mixing. Four additives, labeled Additive J through Additive M, were tested. Every sample used the same batch of powdered solid, the same volume of water, and the same water temperature.

Experiment 1. Enough of one additive was dissolved in 500 mL of water to give a concentration of 5, 10, 15, or 20 mg/L. Next, 2.0 g of the powdered solid was stirred in for 30 s, and a sensor mounted beside the beaker recorded the cloudiness of the sample every 15 s until the cloudiness had fallen below half its starting value. Samples containing no additive were prepared alongside each additive and measured in the same way; their clearing times agreed to within 1 min, and their mean is plotted at 0 mg/L. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Experiment 2. Samples were prepared as in Experiment 1, each containing one additive at 10 mg/L. As soon as the 30 s of mixing ended, half of the samples were left undisturbed (unstirred) and the other half were stirred at 200 rpm for a further 2 min (stirred). The clearing time of each sample was then measured as in Experiment 1. The results are shown in Figure 2.

passage_title: Clearing Time of a Cloudy Suspension Treated with Four Additives
passage:
A powdered solid stirred into water scatters light, so the water looks cloudy. As the particles settle or clump together, the cloudiness falls. Researchers defined the clearing time of a sample as the number of minutes for its cloudiness to fall to half the value measured just after mixing. Four additives, labeled Additive J through Additive M, were tested. Every sample used the same batch of powdered solid, the same volume of water, and the same water temperature.

Experiment 1. Enough of one additive was dissolved in 500 mL of water to give a concentration of 5, 10, 15, or 20 mg/L. Next, 2.0 g of the powdered solid was stirred in for 30 s, and a sensor mounted beside the beaker recorded the cloudiness of the sample every 15 s until the cloudiness had fallen below half its starting value. Samples containing no additive were prepared alongside each additive and measured in the same way; their clearing times agreed to within 1 min, and their mean is plotted at 0 mg/L. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Experiment 2. Samples were prepared as in Experiment 1, each containing one additive at 10 mg/L. As soon as the 30 s of mixing ended, half of the samples were left undisturbed (unstirred) and the other half were stirred at 200 rpm for a further 2 min (stirred). The clearing time of each sample was then measured as in Experiment 1. The results are shown in Figure 2.

passage_title: Clearing Time of a Cloudy Suspension Treated with Four Additives
passage:
A powdered solid stirred into water scatters light, so the water looks cloudy. As the particles settle or clump together, the cloudiness falls. Researchers defined the clearing time of a sample as the number of minutes for its cloudiness to fall to half the value measured just after mixing. Four additives, labeled Additive J through Additive M, were tested. Every sample used the same batch of powdered solid, the same volume of water, and the same water temperature.

Experiment 1. Enough of one additive was dissolved in 500 mL of water to give a concentration of 5, 10, 15, or 20 mg/L. Next, 2.0 g of the powdered solid was stirred in for 30 s, and a sensor mounted beside the beaker recorded the cloudiness of the sample every 15 s until the cloudiness had fallen below half its starting value. Samples containing no additive were prepared alongside each additive and measured in the same way; their clearing times agreed to within 1 min, and their mean is plotted at 0 mg/L. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Experiment 2. Samples were prepared as in Experiment 1, each containing one additive at 10 mg/L. As soon as the 30 s of mixing ended, half of the samples were left undisturbed (unstirred) and the other half were stirred at 200 rpm for a further 2 min (stirred). The clearing time of each sample was then measured as in Experiment 1. The results are shown in Figure 2.

prompt: A student claimed that none of the four additives shortened the clearing time of the powdered solid, relative to the additive-free samples, at any of the additive concentrations tested in Experiment 1. The results in Figure 1 contradict that claim for which additive?
explanation: The additive-free samples are plotted at 0 mg/L, at 12 min. The Additive L curve drops below that level at 5 mg/L and again at 10 mg/L, so for "Additive L" the clearing time was shortened and the claim fails. The Additive J, Additive K and Additive M curves never fall below 12 min at any concentration tested — their lowest plotted values are 21 min, 21 min and 16 min — so "Additive J", "Additive K" and "Additive M" are all consistent with the claim, and choosing one of them means comparing the curves to each other rather than to the additive-free level.
